paragraphs: Friend, look at what this whole chapter is. Israel makes a rash oath, then weeps before God because the oath has backed them into a corner. Then they scramble for a way around it, and every fix they find hurts somebody new: the people of Jabesh-gilead, then the dancing daughters of Shiloh (Judges 21:10-12, 21). I think they were sincere in their grief, but sincere grief did not turn into a good plan.

Here is what the passage is teaching. The elders talk like men with a clever loophole: "Since you did not actually give them your daughters, you have no guilt" (Judges 21:22). Technically clean, friend, and still a mess. When everybody is steering by their own sense of what works, even their tears and their altars can't fix a mess like that.

The book of Judges closes with this: "In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes" (Judges 21:25). It doesn't tie a bow on the story, and I think that's on purpose. It leaves you with an ache for something better than everyone doing their own thing. So here's what I want you to carry out of my bakery, baker: don't trust your own recipe when the whole batch is burning. Look for the One who is worth following, and don't settle for a loophole that only sounds right.
